Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An army of volunteers have been gathering at beaches in the mornings and evenings to help with the cleanup. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian Tyne and Wear ‘There’s no nurdle fairy’: thousands mobilise to clean up plastic spillage in north-east England Volunteers painstakingly gather plastic pellets washing up on beaches after ship collision on 19 July Mark Brown North of England correspondent Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Y ou’ve got a local community that really cares about the coastline,” said Alice Laverty, reflecting on the huge army of volunteers who had taken to crisis-hit beaches in north-east England with passion and only the most basic tools. “They’ve all got a dustpan, a brush, a bucket, a kitchen sieve.” On beaches from Cambois in Northumberland to Seaburn on Wearside, up to 2,000 dedicated volunteers have been painstakingly sifting through sand to find tiny, lentil-sized pellets of plastic. The pellets, called nurdles, are being washed up on beaches after a ship collision on 19 July at the Port of Tyne, South Shields, led to a billion of them spilling into the water . Campaigners estimate there was up to 25 tonnes of them. View image in fullscreen The nurdles are tiny, lentil-sized pellets of plastic. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian The spillage has prompted anger and protests, and the north-east mayor, Kim McGuinness, has promised to make sure shipowners contribute to what she said was a “pollution emergency” . Since the collision, the nurdles have washed up on numerous beaches in the north-east. Some days, nurdle drifts have been like soup, visibly scarring the landscape. Other days, people have had to get down on their hands and knees to find them, but when they do, they’re there. Laverty, a Whitley Bay bookshop owner, was one of the first to respond. “I saw the horrendous pictures of millions of them floating down the Tyne and I went to the beach in the evening,” she said. “I was literally the only person on the beach with a dustpan and brush and I could see people looking at me going … what is she doing?” Volunteers sift beach sands for plastic nurdles - loop Helped by WhatsApp and social media, there is now a more organised army of volunteers gathering at beaches in the mornings and evenings to help with the cleanup. It is a race against the tides and the only way for volunteers to do it is by painstakingly sifting the sand or shaking seaweed. People have been drawing squares and cleaning the beach section by section. “It becomes quite addictive,” Laverty said. “I can’t walk past a nurdle without picking it up, and I reckon most Whitley Bay residents will be exactly the same.” She said a friend told her the story of Aphrodite punishing Psyche by mixing up different grains, seeds and lentils and setting her the impossible task of separating them by dawn. In the story, a sympathetic army of ants comes to the rescue. “Wouldn’t that be great,” she said. View image in fullscreen Alice Laverty: ‘I can’t walk past a nurdle without picking it up.’ Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian The official advice from councils is not to handle the pellets, but Laverty said there was a greater cause. “There’s no nurdle fairy, this needs to be cleaned up now,” she said. “An official response with specialist equipment and trained staff takes time, and concerns about insurance and liability could further delay cleanup operations.” At Whitley Bay beach, the Guardian talked to other volunteers determined to do their bit. Helen Charlton, a business academic from Cramlington, said: “This is our home. I’m north-east born and bred and I’m incredibly proud of this region and I’m incredibly proud of the industry and commerce here as well. It’s not that we shouldn’t have shipping on the Tyne because we absolutely should. But the two have to coexist.” Lou Shackleton, a life and work coach from Whitley Bay, said the nurdles brought multiple dangers. “Everything is interconnected. The people that are fishing need the fish to be there and healthy. The seals need the fish. I heard a boat broke down yesterday because of nurdles affecting the engine. It’s the summer holidays, there’ll be people in the sea, kids playing. “I have a five-year-old, I don’t want him to be still finding nurdles on the beach in 10 years’ time.” View image in fullscreen Volunteers search for nurdles. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian Amy Ash, a user experience designer, has created a web app to help organise and mobilise the volunteers . “I surf, I swim, I’ve got two kids,” she said. “It is absolutely devastating that these things are on the beach. I really do not want this to be forgotten about.” As well as the sweepers and sifters, dozens of volunteers have been sewing together mesh bags for collecting the nurdles using scaffolding fabric. Nurdles are tiny disc-shaped plastic pellets that act as the raw material to manufacture most plastic products. Animals can easily mistake them for food with deadly consequences, campaigners say. The environmental charity Fidra , which works to end plastic and chemical pollution, says nurdles are a global problem. Last year it found plastic nurdles at 84% of the UK’s sites of special scientific interest . The Port of Tyne, HM Coastguard, the Environment Agency, local councils and specialist contractors are all involved in what has been called “a coordinated multi-agency effort” to clean up after the spill. By Sunday, about 3,000 volunteer hours had been logged and an estimated 285kg of nurdles had been recovered by the “people’s army”. An open letter is due to be sent on Monday calling for trained local teams to be allowed to help clear nurdles directly from the rivers, not just the beaches. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Any Burnham has said there should be ‘greater public control’ of Thames Water. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock Thames Water Thames Water creditors accused of ‘shuffling deckchairs’ with plan for new board Campaigners say proposal for £10bn rescue deal in bid to avoid nationalisation is a ‘cosy stitch-up’ Business live – latest updates Alex Daniel Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.38 EDT First published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The group of creditors pursuing a rescue bid for Thames Water have been accused of shuffling the deckchairs on the Titanic after proposing an overhaul of the stricken utility’s board. In a bid to stave off temporary nationalisation by Andy Burnham, the lenders said they would appoint Liz Barber, the former chief executive of Yorkshire Water , and Clive Selley, the former chief executive of network operator Openreach, as directors if they are allowed to take formal control of the company. London & Valley Water (L&VW), a consortium of 100 institutional investors holding £17bn of the company’s £21bn debt, has also lined up Dame Bernadette Kelly, the former permanent secretary of the Department for Transport. Thames Water plans to restart desalination plant – after drought has ended Read more Mike McTighe, the corporate troubleshooter leading Thames’s overhaul, would become the new chair, replacing the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if Thames is able to get its £10bn rescue deal approved by the government. McTighe is the current chair of Openreach. He said: “The challenge at Thames Water is huge. If this recapitalisation plan is accepted, we will apply full dedication as a new board, working alongside the executive team to transform the business and build a culture in which the customers and local communities who depend on Thames Water come first.” The proposed appointments are designed to reassure the government that any commercial deal would bring with it a leadership overhaul, as Burnham’s team examines the possibility of taking the company back into public ownership. L&VW’s announcement was criticised by the public ownership campaign group We Own It. Cat Hobbs, the director at We Own It, said: “This is absolutely absurd. A cosy stitch-up that has nothing to do with the interests of the 16 million people who depend on Thames Water. This amounts to nothing more than a reshuffling of chairs on the deck of the Titanic.” Burnham has said there should be “greater public control” of Thames Water and previously told the Guardian this could mean nationalisation. This would probably come via placing the company into a special administration regime (SAR), a form of temporary nationalisation. More recently the prime minister said he was “angry” after companies including Thames Water were given the green light to raise bills even higher earlier this month. He said the companies must not be allowed to treat bill payers like a “blank cheque”, an escalation of his warnings to utility companies that he is looking at options for more government control of the sector. The SAR proposal would transfer the costs of running the company to the taxpayer, with Thames Water claiming the bill could come to £2bn. L&VW, which includes fund managers such as Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital, has also moved to strengthen its legal position in order to be prepared if Thames is nationalised. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The consortium has hired the top litigation and disputes lawyers Pallas Partners to work alongside Akin Gump, the law firm advising the consortium on the terms of their restructuring proposals. The lenders have been trying to take ownership and bring Thames out of administration after a failed attempt to sell the utility to the US investment group KKR last year. However, the creditors’ plans were thrown into doubt in June when Emma Reynolds, the then environment secretary, wrote to the regulator, Ofwat, voicing concerns about the terms of the deal . McTighe said the 10-year plan to turn the water company around would “fix the foundations” at Thames. “It will take time to fix Thames Water, but we are committed to rebuilding trust with the customers and public Thames Water serves,” he said. Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell, said of the proposed new appointments: “The hope being that these are the sort of credible names which can inspire confidence in the company’s future in private hands. “Such an outcome would impose large losses on creditors, who are seeking to formally take ownership of the business, having already assumed de facto control, with plans to list it on the stock market as early as 2030.” Explore more on these topics Thames Water Water Utilities news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Thames Water plans to restart desalination plant – after drought has ended Thames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government department Burnham has forced greater clarity at Thames Water. http://www.president.go.ke/kenya-to-open.text: KENYA TO OPEN EMBASSY IN HUNGARY’S CAPITAL March 7, 2023 President William Ruto has directed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Diaspora to open an embassy in Budapest, Hungary. The President said the process should begin immediately and the Mission be up in a year or two. Speaking when he hosted the Speaker of the Hungarian Parliament, Dr László Kövér, at State House Nairobi, President Ruto said the embassy will help escalate the relations between our two countries. The President thanked the Hungarian Government for Ksh6.2 billion support that will go into the setting up of the Dedan Kimathi Comprehensive Cancer Management in Nyeri. The funds will also go into the establishment of the Kabonyo Regional Service and Training Centre of Excellence and the rehabilitation of the Ahero Irrigation Scheme in Kisumu County. On climate change, President Ruto said Kenya has taken a “robust position at international fora” on the critical matter because the phenomenon poses an existential threat to humanity. “The world is at a crossroads: Do we continue with fossil fuels and burn the globe or do we go the clean energy route and save the world,” he said. On his part, the Hungarian Speaker said the parliaments of the two countries have done a lot in strengthening the relations between Kenya and Hungary. Dr Kövér concurred with the President that Hungary is keen in mitigating the effects of climate change. Kenya exports to Hungary include cut flowers, fruits, vegetables, tobacco and fish. There are more opportunities in meat, clothing, dairy and pharmaceutical products. https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: KYIV — With another bitter winter of fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war ahead, diplomatic activity is ramping back up in a fresh attempt to close in on a ceasefire and eventually a final peace accord. Under renewed pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, Kyiv and Moscow are preparing to send negotiating teams to Abu Dhabi for a three-way meeting with American officials to explore the potential for agreement. The meeting is penciled in for Nov. 10. But many questions about the process remain, including whether Europe will have a seat at the table when key decisions are taken — and who should fill it. Based on remarks from key leaders, and conversations with European officials granted anonymity because the talks are sensitive, POLITICO breaks down what's under discussion for an agreement and what could get in the way. Advertisement Advertisement What will they discuss? Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the agenda for Abu Dhabi should first include initial steps toward de-escalation, such as prisoner swaps and ceasefires on energy infrastructure and for the Black Sea. There should also be a discussion among the technical negotiating teams of what format a future three-way meeting between leaders — Trump, Zelenskyy and Russia’s Vladimir Putin — should take, he told reporters this week. When it comes to a final deal, one overriding question for Ukraine is what form of security guarantees it will get from Europe and the U.S., or potentially NATO. Zelenskyy won't want to accept anything he believes could leave Ukraine vulnerable to a future attack from Russia. Putin is also likely to raise the need for security guarantees — for Russia — including limiting or potentially reversing NATO’s presence in the neighborhood. Then there’s the question of territory. Zelenskyy’s view is that marking out any boundaries, temporarily or permanently, is something that can only be discussed at leader level. “No one else has the authority to do so,” he said Tuesday. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press briefing at the Catshuis in the Hague on October 28, 2026. | Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP via Getty Images Zelenskyy said during previous sets of negotiations over the past year, “as a compromise,” that Ukraine had been prepared to discuss the idea of a demilitarized “buffer zone” on both sides of the contact line in the Donbas region. Similar ideas were proposed for other parts of Ukraine. Zelenskyy said his negotiators discussed these questions again with the Americans in recent weeks. “We are ready to discuss the issue of territories because the Russians keep wanting to discuss it and make it part of the agenda,” he said. But this would need to be at a leader-level meeting. Advertisement Advertisement Europe has a role European leaders are adamant that they must be included in final negotiations, not least because it is they who are are now providing the vast bulk of financial and military support to Ukraine. Trump ended American aid in 2025. Zelenskyy and U.S. officials accept that European governments will likely need to be involved in discussions about security guarantees — mainly because any peacekeeping forces deployed to Ukraine would be dominated by European troops. The Coalition of the Willing, a loose alliance of more than 30 countries led by France, the U.K. and Germany, put together detailed proposals in coordination with the U.S. almost a year ago. Ukraine is also interested in exploring bilateral security guarantees with the U.S., a discussion that would not need to involve European officials. Moldova's President Maia Sandu, President of the European Council Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Lithuania's President Gitanas Nauseda and Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs react as they attend the Coalition of the Willing meeting, in Kyiv on August 24, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images Plans for rebuilding Ukraine and nurturing its economic revival would also have to involve Europe, Zelenskyy said. "We cannot envision such a, so to speak, ‘Marshall Plan’ without Europe." But Europe doesn’t know who should speak for it Trump’s renewed interest in Ukraine also resurfaced some sore questions for European governments: Who should represent them when it comes to decision time? And should they even be talking to Putin at all? With no clarity emerging from Brussels, some leaders have taken matters into their own hands. On Tuesday, Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a 90-minute call with Putin, urging him to end the war. It went down badly with several European governments, including Denmark, Italy, Sweden and Lithuania. One frustrated diplomat said: “There are too many middle-aged men who want to end up in the history books having solved this war.” Advertisement Advertisement Russia has said the Stubb-Støre call achieved nothing of substance and the war will likely “escalate.” By some accounts, Putin used much of the time on the phone lecturing the Nordic leaders on regional history. One problem in identifying a lead negotiator is that the European countries with a stake in the talks are not only in the EU — the U.K. and Norway, for example, are both outside the bloc. Without clarity of leadership, European interests risk being sidelined when the talking gets serious. It all comes down to Trump One critical unknown factor in the mix is how long Trump's attention will stay on Ukraine. After the U.S. and Israel launched a war with Iran in the spring, progress on Ukraine stalled for months, only to return this fall as Trump sought to mitigate the impact of the Middle East conflict. A new escalation in the Iran war risks sidelining the negotiations all over again. The U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Zelenskyy, Stubb and Støre in Oslo on Oct. 20. Witkoff then went to St. Petersburg to meet Putin the next day. There was supposed to be a follow-up meeting in Brussels this week in preparation for negotiations in Abu Dhabi — but the Americans postponed the talks, apparently due to developments in the Middle East. “The meeting in Abu Dhabi now depends on the American side,” Zelenskyy said Tuesday. At a press conference Wednesday, he added: “We very much hope that the escalatory processes in the Middle East — which are currently the subject of so much discussion — will not interfere." Advertisement Advertisement Putin can wait After their Kremlin call, Stubb and Støre apparently told Zelenskyy they felt Putin was serious about the Abu Dhabi opportunity. But in public and private, diplomats and political leaders in Europe are deeply skeptical that Putin is at all serious about an imminent path to peace. Despite the Kremlin insisting he is on board, European diplomats believe the Russian leader is just playing for time in the hope that Ukraine weakens over a winter of attacks on its energy system, and Europe — perhaps with the far-right Marine Le Pen in charge of France — gets tired of paying for the war and gives up next year. That’s why EU officials know they cannot pin their hopes on peace and need to redouble their financial support and military aid for Ukraine, while tightening sanctions on Russia. EU leaders will discuss the issue of securing funds for Ukraine’s war effort at their summit in Brussels scheduled for November 26. Nicholas Vinocur in Brussels contributed to this report .

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: A demonstrator is removed by police during a protest in support of Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Sunday. Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A demonstrator is removed by police during a protest in support of Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Sunday. Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty Images UK news Almost 50 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in London Met alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in first such gathering under Burnham Sammy Gecsoyler Sat 31 Oct 2026 12.38 EDT First published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Almost 50 people have been arrested at the first mass demonstrations under Andy Burnham’s premiership opposing the proscription of Palestine Action. Hundreds of people gathered outside the US embassy in Battersea, south London, holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Demonstrators also held a vigil in support of the group outside the US consulate in Edinburgh. Before the London gathering, the Metropolitan police warned those taking part “that they face arrest as part of a robust policing operation” and that anyone “playing a key role in organising the event, giving instructions to others and/or providing logistical support” would probably be committing an offence. In a statement on X, the Metropolitan police said: “So far this afternoon, officers have arrested 48 people.” Commander Adam Slonecki, who is leading the policing operation, said: “All those intending on coming to this event know that supporting a proscribed organisation is unlawful – they are essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime. Defend Our Juries, the group behind the demonstrations, said the Met was “terrified of facilitating US embarrassment” and estimated that “around 400 people” gathered to take part. Among those sitting outside the US embassy, holding a sign that appeared to express support for Palestine Action, was Sue Morhall. “The USA is complicit in most of the wars that are going on. I just feel the leaders of this world, including Trump, need to know that people are so against what’s happening in Gaza,” said the 79-year-old retiree. View image in fullscreen Sue Morhall takes part in the demonstration outside the US embassy in London. Morhall believes there is a chance Burnham could rescind the proscription. “I think it’s early days. I’m hopeful, though pigs might fly,” she said. “I think he’s going to perhaps wait until the midterm elections in America. It’s a terrible shame that people who are trying to stop a genocide are being arrested.” She has been arrested “five or six” times at previous demonstrations and feels “OK” about being hauled into a police van again. “It’s the principle, and this is one that I feel very strongly about,” she said. The Rev Bill White, 72, who also held a sign that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” said: “I’m appalled that Britain is helping facilitate the genocide that is happening in Palestine. We supply weapons that are being used on Palestinians.” View image in fullscreen Rev Bill White also took part in the demonstration. He said he had “hoped for better” from Burnham and resigned from the Labour party after Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist group. As a faith leader, he said there was “no choice” other than to take part in the demonstration. “This is the right thing to do. There’s a bad law and it is wrong to criminalise people that are trying to prevent genocide,” he said. “How can I not be here?” A Defend Our Juries spokesperson said: “The Met police overzealous response outside the US embassy today only serves to further expose how far authorities in the UK will go to appease American interests. Israel’s war crimes that have caused death and injury to thousands could not happen without the US’s approval.” The protests come before an appeal at the UK supreme court against Palestine Action’s designation as a terror group on 4 November. Last month, more than 160 people were arrested or reported for summons at a similar demonstration in support of Palestine Action staged outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool. The new government has come under pressure to rescind the ban, though Shabana Mahmood, who has stood firm in favour of the group’s proscription, remained in post as home secretary. The journalist and author Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, was accused of supporting Palestine Action after posting on X : “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.” Her post came in response to news that the Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the group. During the Labour party conference, two activists confronted the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, during a meal at Pizza Express in the city centre where he was challenged about the arrests. Video of the incident showed one of the protesters urging Miliband to declare a genocide in Gaza and de-proscribe Palestine Action. Miliband said he was happy to discuss the issue but at another time, before the protesters were ushered out. One woman, who held a sign that, bar swapping the word “authors” to “retirees”, replicated the X post by Sarah Helm, was among those arrested in London, despite the Met ultimately assessing that Helm’s post “did not meet the criminal threshold”.
